items.title: The Human-AI Substitution Principle: When will you be replaced by AI in your organization?
items.summary:
arXiv:2607.20781v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming organizations, raising a fundamental organizational and economic question: when will a human employee be replaced by AI? We present an analytical model for studying Human--AI Task Allocation (HAT) in hierarchical organizations. A central feature of the HAT model is that it formally encodes the economic asymmetry between human skill acquisition and AI capability scaling. The HAT model allows us to derive how risk-adjusted costs, skills, organizational depth, deployment scale, strategic adaptation, and risk jointly determine when, where, why, and under what structural conditions human--AI replacement occurs. A key result is the Human--AI Substitution Principle, which provides a precise condition --- grounded in the formal asymmetry assumption --- under which AI replaces human labor. Building on this result, we show that AI adoption can produce abrupt workforce transitions, hybrid human--AI organizations, including cases where risk heterogeneity sustains human and AI roles without requiring a minimum-human-fraction constraint, and flatter managerial hierarchies with wider spans of control. The HAT model identifies structural conditions under which middle-management roles exhibit elevated vulnerability to automation, and shows that the vulnerability of highly skilled workers depends on a skill threshold shaped by organizational depth, baseline costs, and risk differentials. More broadly, the paper connects automation economics, organizational design, AI governance, and workforce planning into a unified theory of AI-driven organizational transformation.
items.claude_summary: When does AI replace a human worker, and under what organizational conditions? This paper presents a formal model of Human-AI Task Allocation (HAT) in hierarchical organizations, deriving a precise 'substitution principle' based on the economic asymmetry between human skill acquisition (costly and slow) and AI capability scaling (cheaper and faster). The model predicts that AI adoption can produce abrupt workforce transitions rather than gradual ones, that middle-management roles face elevated vulnerability, and that highly skilled workers are protected only up to a threshold shaped by organizational depth and risk differentials. The analysis also suggests AI flattens hierarchies and widens managerial spans of control. The paper is a working paper from arXiv and has not yet undergone peer review.
items.centre_angle: This paper derives formal conditions under which AI substitutes for human labor across organizational layers, finding that middle management faces structural — not merely incidental — vulnerability, and that even highly skilled workers lose protection once AI capability crosses a threshold shaped by organizational depth. From CAMO's perspective on AI and jobs, the result complements our own work on job design: the 'bad job economy' paper (Toward a Bad Job Economy) shows a parallel mechanism whereby AI lowers the cost of satisfactory performance and induces firms to replace high-effort roles, and the HAT model here offers a complementary structural account of where those replacements concentrate in a hierarchy. Together, both lines of work suggest that the workforce risk from AI is not uniform across levels — it is shaped by organizational architecture, cost asymmetries, and incentive design simultaneously.

matched_camo.title: Toward a Bad Job Economy: AI Adoption, Agency Costs, and Job Design
matched_camo.reason: Both papers model how AI's cost asymmetry relative to human labor reshapes which roles firms sustain, with overlapping predictions about downward pressure on wages, job quality, and the conditions under which AI substitutes rather than complements workers.

items.key_takeaway: AI replacement in organizations is not random — it concentrates in middle management and follows a predictable structural logic tied to cost asymmetries, organizational depth, and risk, meaning firms can anticipate vulnerability hot-spots rather than react to them.
items.visual_concept: A single tall organizational chart rendered as a vertical architectural cross-section — like a narrow building cut open to reveal its floors — positioned slightly left of center in a wide frame. Each floor represents a hierarchical layer, with the middle floors visually thinner and structurally stressed, as if under compression. A single sharp diagonal leading line descends from the upper-right corner of the frame toward the compressed middle floors, drawing the eye to the vulnerability zone. The upper and lower floors remain solid and intact. The surrounding environment is minimal — a flat neutral grey ground plane and a cool, diffuse blue-grey light falling from above, creating soft shadows that pool at the middle section. The palette is cool and desaturated with one muted amber accent highlighting the stressed middle tier, suggesting structural risk without alarm.
red_flags: Preprint only — posted to arXiv, not yet peer-reviewed; findings should be treated as preliminary.

The model's empirical grounding is not verifiable from the abstract alone; key assumptions (e.g., the formal asymmetry between human skill acquisition and AI scaling) are asserted rather than tested against organizational data.
Broad theoretical claims (abrupt transitions, hierarchy flattening) are derived analytically and may not translate cleanly to empirical settings without calibration.

items.title: From Obligation to Specification: A Survey on Validating EU AI Act Requirements in RE
items.authors: T. Y. Emmy Lai, Sven Giesselbach, Matthias Koch, H\'ector Allende-Cid
items.summary:
arXiv:2607.21608v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: With the EU AI Act entering into force, organizations developing or operating AI systems face new obligations on transparency, risk management, and traceability. For Requirements Engineering (RE), these obligations must be translated into testable, auditable requirements and verifiable evidence. However, many organizations currently lack systematic processes to achieve this. We hypothesize that LLM-based agentic validation tools can support this translation, thereby helping to close this gap. We present a mixed-method exploratory study with expert interviews (N=10) and an online survey (N=15) to assess organizational preparedness for EU AI Act-oriented RE and perceptions of LLM-based, agentic closed-loop validation tools, with participants spanning RE, data science, development, and compliance roles. Our results show that, although the EU AI Act is viewed as highly relevant, structured mechanisms to capture regulatory obligations, propagate updates into projects, and maintain lifecycle-wide traceability and evidence are often missing. Participants see LLM-based tools as promising for mapping obligations to requirements, assessing coverage, and organizing evidence, but express strong concerns about full automation and stress the need for safeguards. Based on these findings, we outline minimum requirements for an EU AI Act-ready closed-loop approach.
items.claude_summary: As the EU AI Act moves from principle to enforcement, organizations building or deploying AI systems face a concrete operational gap: they lack systematic processes to translate regulatory obligations—on transparency, risk management, and traceability—into testable engineering requirements. A mixed-method study combining expert interviews and a survey finds that awareness of the Act is high, but structured mechanisms for capturing obligations, propagating regulatory updates across projects, and maintaining lifecycle-wide evidence trails are largely absent. Participants see LLM-based validation tools as promising for mapping obligations to requirements and organizing evidence, but resist full automation and call for meaningful human oversight safeguards. The study proposes minimum design requirements for a compliant, closed-loop requirements engineering approach.
items.centre_angle: This survey argues that EU AI Act compliance is primarily an organizational and process failure, not a technical one: firms understand the regulation but lack the internal workflows to operationalize it into auditable engineering requirements. From CAMO's perspective on AI Adoption, this mirrors a pattern documented in the Deloitte-HKU AI Adoption Index—where the dominant barriers to effective AI deployment are executional and structural rather than technological. The implication for managers is that regulatory readiness requires investing in governance architecture and cross-functional processes, not simply procuring compliance tools.

matched_camo.reason: Both studies find that organizations' AI ambitions are undermined not by technology gaps but by organizational and executional deficiencies—siloed processes, missing governance structures, and the absence of systematic internal mechanisms.

items.key_takeaway: Most organizations developing AI systems under the EU AI Act are aware of their obligations but lack the internal processes to convert those obligations into auditable engineering requirements—a gap that poses real compliance risk.
items.visual_concept: A single printed regulatory document, centered and slightly off-axis in the lower-left third of the frame, its pages fanned open to reveal dense text on one side and a sparse, half-completed checklist on the other. The document rests on a plain light-grey desk surface with nothing else competing for attention. A narrow shaft of cool, diffused daylight enters from the upper-right corner, pooling directly onto the checklist side of the open document and leaving the dense text page in soft shadow—visually reinforcing the gap between obligation and specification. The background is a clean, slightly out-of-focus architectural wall in off-white, conveying an institutional setting without clutter. Palette is muted: cool greys and whites with a faint blue cast, suggesting precision and process rather than urgency.

Small sample sizes (N=10 interviews, N=15 survey) limit generalizability; findings are exploratory by the authors' own description.
Participant pool is not fully described in the excerpt, raising questions about industry and geographic diversity.
The study's hypothesis that LLM-based tools can close the compliance gap is partially self-serving as a research framing; evidence presented is perceptual, not empirical performance data.

items.title: Developing and Validating the Spanish Version of the Large Language Models Dependency Scale (LLM-D12-SP)
items.authors: Tran Gia Bao, Mo El-Haj, Sameha Al-Shakhsi, Antonio Garcia-Cabot, Raian Ali, Ala Yankouskaya
items.summary:
arXiv:2607.22041v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: There is a growing need for reliable and culturally validated instruments to assess psychological dependency on large language models (LLMs), particularly as LLMs are increasingly used for task execution, decision-making, and communication in organizational and work-related settings. This need is especially relevant for Spanish-speaking populations, where LLM adoption is rapidly expanding, yet validated psychometric tools remain scarce. The present study reports the first validation of the Spanish version of the Large Language Model Dependency Scale (LLM-D12-SP), extending prior validations conducted in English- and Arabic-speaking samples. The LLM-D12 is a two-dimensional instrument assessing Instrumental Dependency (reliance on LLMs for performing tasks and supporting decisions) and Relationship Dependency (psychological reliance on LLMs for companionship and social interaction). A total of 386 Spanish-speaking participants (M = 28.0 years, SD = 6.1; 55% male) completed the LLM-D12-SP. Confirmatory factor analysis supported the original two-factor structure. The scale demonstrated good internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha = 0.89 total; 0.86 Instrumental; 0.85 Relationship). Discriminant validity analyses indicated that the two subscales represent related but distinct constructs. External validation showed that both dependency dimensions were positively associated with internet addiction and perceived trustworthiness of LLMs, while showing weak or no association with need for cognition. Together with prior English and Arabic validations, these findings establish cross-linguistic support for the scale's structure and provide a psychometrically sound tool for investigating psychological aspects of LLM use in organizational contexts.
items.claude_summary: As large language models become standard tools for task execution and decision-making at work, researchers have developed and validated a Spanish-language psychometric scale to measure psychological dependency on LLMs. The LLM-D12-SP distinguishes two forms of dependency: instrumental (relying on LLMs to perform tasks and inform decisions) and relational (turning to LLMs for companionship and social interaction). Tested on 386 Spanish-speaking participants, the scale showed strong internal consistency and confirmed that both dependency dimensions correlate with internet addiction and perceived trustworthiness of LLMs, but not with need for cognition. This cross-linguistic validation extends prior English and Arabic versions, offering organizations a standardized tool to diagnose how deeply, and in what ways, employees are psychologically anchored to LLM tools.
items.centre_angle: This study introduces a validated instrument for measuring two distinct forms of LLM dependency—task-oriented reliance and social-psychological reliance—among Spanish-speaking users. From CAMO's perspective on AI adoption, the more practically urgent finding is that instrumental dependency (using LLMs as a decision-making crutch) is now measurable at the individual level, which opens the door to assessing whether organizational AI adoption is building genuine capability or deepening unhealthy over-reliance. The scale's weak correlation with need for cognition is worth noting: employees who depend most on LLMs are not simply those who prefer not to think hard, suggesting dependency is shaped more by workflow design and perceived tool trustworthiness than by individual cognitive disposition.

matched_camo.title: The Double-Edged Sword of Mandatory AI Adoption at a Leading Medical Device Firm
matched_camo.reason: Both pieces grapple with the quality of employee engagement with AI tools—whether use reflects genuine reliance or superficial compliance—and the organizational consequences of that distinction.

items.key_takeaway: Organizations now have a cross-linguistically validated tool to distinguish whether employees depend on LLMs as a decision aid or as a social substitute—a meaningful difference for workforce design and AI governance.
items.visual_concept: A single wooden desk, centered slightly left of frame and filling the foreground, with a closed laptop sitting on it as the focal object. Soft, cool morning light from an unseen window falls directly onto the laptop lid, casting a long shadow toward the lower-right corner of the frame that draws the eye back to the desk's surface. The background is a plain, slightly out-of-focus office wall with no decoration—nothing competes with the desk and laptop. The palette is muted grey-blue with warm amber wood tones on the desk surface. The mood is still and ambiguous: the closed laptop suggests both presence and absence, dependency and restraint.
red_flags: Not yet peer-reviewed — posted as arXiv preprint; findings should be treated as preliminary until published in a refereed journal.
Sample is relatively young (mean age 28) and self-selected, which may limit generalizability to broader organizational populations.
The article is primarily a psychometric validation study; its direct implications for organizational management are inferential rather than empirically demonstrated.

items.title: How Can AI Augment Access to Justice? Public Defenders' Perspectives on AI Adoption
items.authors: Inyoung Cheong, Patty Liu, Dominik Stammbach, Peter Henderson
items.summary:
arXiv:2510.22933v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Public defenders are asked to do more with less: representing clients deserving of adequate counsel while facing overwhelming caseloads and scarce resources. Although artificial intelligence (AI) is often promoted as a means of relieving administrative and cognitive burdens, legal AI research rarely engages with the everyday realities of public defense work. Drawing on in-depth, semi-structured interviews with 17 public defense professionals across the United States, we identify work-intensive tasks most amenable to AI assistance and the ethical constraints involved in legal representation. We develop a comprehensive task-level map of public defense work, dividing it into five pillars to clarify where AI can and cannot contribute: evidence investigation, legal research & writing, client communication & support, courtroom representation, and defense strategies. Interviewees consistently identified evidence investigation, such as reviewing large volumes of digital records, as the area with the greatest potential for AI support. AI was viewed as having more limited roles in legal research and client communication, and as least compatible with courtroom representation and defense strategy. We find that AI adoption is constrained by costs, restrictive office norms, confidentiality risks, and unsatisfactory tool quality. Our interviewees emphasize safeguards for responsible use, including mandatory human verification, limits on over-reliance, and the preservation of relational aspects of lawyering. Building on these findings, we outline a research agenda that promotes equitable access to justice by prioritizing open science, building domain-specific datasets and evaluation, and incorporating frontline practitioners' perspectives into system development.
items.claude_summary: Public defenders in the United States face crushing caseloads with limited resources, and this study asks where AI can realistically help. Drawing on interviews with 17 public defense professionals, the researchers map legal defense work into five domains and find that AI is most useful for reviewing large volumes of digital evidence. Its role is more limited in legal research and client communication, and largely incompatible with courtroom representation and defense strategy. Adoption is held back by cost, confidentiality risks, restrictive office norms, and tool quality. Practitioners emphasize that responsible use requires human verification and protecting the relational dimensions of lawyering. The paper closes with a research agenda focused on open science and practitioner-informed tool development.
items.centre_angle: This study shows that AI adoption in high-stakes professional settings is not primarily a technical problem — it is an organizational and ethical one. Public defenders accept AI for narrow, well-bounded tasks such as document review, but resist it where professional judgment, client trust, and accountability cannot be delegated. From CAMO's perspective on AI adoption, this mirrors the pattern documented in our C-suite survey work: the dominant barriers to adoption are organizational and executional rather than technical. The study also raises a question directly relevant to CAMO's research on job design — as AI absorbs document-heavy work, what happens to the skills, career trajectories, and accountability structures of lawyers who no longer build those competencies through practice?

matched_camo.reason: Both studies find that AI adoption stalls not because the technology is absent but because organizational norms, trust deficits, and cultural resistance block genuine integration — a structural parallel even across very different sectors.

matched_camo.title: Research: The Hidden Penalty of Using AI at Work
matched_camo.reason: Both papers surface social and reputational risks that discourage professionals from using AI tools even when the tools could be helpful, pointing to a mismatch between institutional incentives and adoption.

items.key_takeaway: AI can relieve the document-review burden on under-resourced public defenders, but cost, confidentiality, and professional accountability norms are the real gatekeepers to adoption — not the technology itself.

items.title: How a Museum Marketing Team Used AI to Bring People Closer to Art
items.summary: In 2025, Harvard Art Museums considered using generative AI in a marketing campaign to increase visitor engagement and membership. Looking to boost attendance and appeal to a younger audience base, and facing intensified competition for leisure time, the Museums’ marketing team explored animating a canonical artwork using AI-generated avatars as part of a digital campaign. While the approach promised novelty and attention, it raised internal concerns about brand authenticity, interpretive authority, donor relations, and reputational risk. Harvard Business School Assistant Professor Julian De Freitas and Harvard Art Museums Director of Marketing John Connolly join host Brian Kenny to discuss the case, Harvard Art Museums: When Art Meets Artificial Intelligence. They explore tensions between innovation and brand stewardship in cultural marketing, organizational barriers to new technology adoption, and the strategic use of emerging technologies in brand management.
items.claude_summary: When Harvard Art Museums explored using AI-generated avatars to animate a canonical artwork for a digital marketing campaign, the initiative surfaced tensions that go well beyond marketing strategy. The team weighed potential gains in visitor engagement and appeal to younger audiences against concerns about brand authenticity, interpretive authority, donor relations, and reputational risk. The case — discussed by HBS Assistant Professor Julian De Freitas and the Museums' Director of Marketing — illustrates how cultural institutions face organizational and ethical friction when adopting generative AI, even in relatively low-stakes applications. The excerpt is from a podcast discussion of an HBS case study rather than an empirical research paper, so specific findings are limited.
items.centre_angle: This case illustrates how even a modest generative AI pilot — animating a single artwork for a marketing campaign — can stall not for technical reasons but because of unresolved organizational questions about authority, brand stewardship, and stakeholder trust. CAMO's research on AI adoption consistently finds that the dominant barriers are cultural and executional rather than technical; the Harvard Art Museums case adds a dimension specific to mission-driven organizations, where brand identity and interpretive legitimacy complicate the cost-benefit calculus that drives adoption in commercial firms. The tension between innovation appetite and institutional caution shown here echoes findings from the Deloitte-HKU AI Adoption Index, which identified cultural resistance and unclear ownership as leading reasons why AI initiatives fall short of expected returns.

matched_camo.title: Deloitte-HKU AI Adoption Index 2026: The Paradox of Promise and Performance
matched_camo.reason: Both the case and the Index highlight how organizational and cultural resistance — rather than technical capability — are the central obstacles to moving AI pilots forward.

items.key_takeaway: For mission-driven organizations, the hardest AI adoption questions are not technical but institutional — who owns the brand, who interprets the work, and what risks are acceptable to take with reputation.
items.visual_concept: A single large gilt-framed painting centered on the wall of an otherwise spare, high-ceilinged gallery, lit by a narrow overhead spotlight that pools warm amber light onto the canvas while the surrounding walls recede into cool shadow. In the immediate foreground, slightly off-center to the left, a small tablet or screen rests face-up on a plain white plinth, its faint cool-blue glow contrasting with the warm painting behind it — the sole indicator of digital presence without depicting any AI iconography. No quantitative data or outcomes reported in the excerpt; article may be primarily narrative and practitioner-facing.

items.title: Leadership Summit 2026: Inspiring Grit and Growth Amid Unprecedented Change
items.summary: Most leaders are asking the same question about AI: Will it make their teams more productive—or slowly erode the very skills they're trying to build? In this special episode, as part of the recent HBR Leadership Summit 2026, University of Pennsylvania's Angela Duckworth says her long-standing research on grit—and the fact the most successful people aren't simply persistent, they stay committed to long-term goals while adapting their tactics as the world changes—is more relevant than ever in the age of generative AI. Rather than replacing human capability, she explains, AI can become a powerful coach that accelerates learning, if people treat it as something to learn from, not simply something that does the work for them. Duckworth’s new book is Situated: Find the People and Places That Bring Out Your Best.
items.claude_summary: Angela Duckworth, speaking at the HBR Leadership Summit 2026, argues that her research on grit—sustained commitment to long-term goals while adapting tactics—becomes more important, not less, in the generative AI era. The central question she addresses is whether AI will build or erode the skills of the people using it. Her answer depends on how people relate to the technology: AI used as a passive executor of tasks undermines skill development, while AI used as an active coach can accelerate learning. The excerpt is thin on empirical data and draws primarily on Duckworth's existing grit research rather than new findings on AI specifically.
items.centre_angle: This podcast episode raises a motivational question that sits at the center of organizational AI adoption: when AI reduces the effort required to produce acceptable output, does it also reduce the effortful practice through which genuine skill is built? From CAMO's perspective on AI and incentives, this is not merely a mindset question but a structural one. CAMO's experimental work on generative AI and professional illustrators ('Better Technology, Worse Motivation') found precisely this dynamic in action—AI assistance flattened the quality curve and led a significant share of professionals to trade final quality for time savings, a strategic response to diminished returns on sustained effort. Duckworth's prescription that individuals should treat AI as something to learn from, rather than something that does the work, is intuitively appealing, but organizational incentive structures may work against it unless firms deliberately design for high-effort, high-growth engagement rather than minimum-viable-output efficiency.

matched_camo.title: Better Technology, Worse Motivation: GenAI and the Mediocrity Trap
matched_camo.reason: Both the podcast and this paper address how AI assistance can undermine sustained effort and the motivation for excellence, with the paper providing experimental evidence for the mechanism Duckworth warns about.

items.key_takeaway: AI strengthens skills only when workers treat it as a learning tool—but organizations must design incentives that make effortful engagement worth the effort, or individuals will rationally default to 'good enough.'

items.title: Unfit for stranding assessment: a panel-scale multimodal-LLM audit of building-decarbonisation disclosure (BeDA)
items.authors: Jingyi Xu, Minghui Cheng, Anchen Sun
items.summary:
arXiv:2607.22006v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Buildings account for roughly 34% of global final energy use and 37% of energy- and process-related CO$_2$ emissions. Stranding regulation now being enacted (New York City Local Law 97, the EU Energy Performance of Buildings Directive recast) presupposes that a building portfolio's carbon intensity can be measured per square metre and compared against a science-based pathway. Whether corporate disclosure is actually fit for that comparison has not, to our knowledge, been measured at scale. We introduce BeDA (the Built-environment Decarbonisation-disclosure Auditor), a multimodal large-language-model instrument, and apply it to a global firm panel (2,246 firms, 2003-2023). Its standards-compliance score is reliable across models and model families and convergent with three independent external criteria. Most disclosure is unfit: only about one built-environment firm-report in five discloses operational carbon intensity per $m^2$ (21.5% in a region-stratified sample of 200 firm-reports, Wilson 95% CI [16.4%, 27.7%], inter-extractor $\kappa$=0.95; 45.5% across 519 real-estate firm-reports, $\kappa$=0.97). The rate is roughly twice as high in Europe as in the United States (64-74% versus 37% for listed real estate). Among the 215 real-estate firm-reports for which an intensity can be constructed, 39% already exceed the Carbon Risk Real Estate Monitor (CRREM) 1.5 {\deg}C pathway's intensity limit. Credibility does not predict stranding readiness once portfolio size is controlled; this is a screening tool, not a forecast. The main obstacle to enforceable building-stranding regulation is therefore a measurable, jurisdiction-specific reporting gap, one that a targeted disclosure mandate can close and that BeDA can monitor.
items.claude_summary: Buildings generate 37% of energy-related CO₂ emissions, and new regulations in New York and the EU now require firms to report carbon intensity per square metre for comparison against science-based decarbonisation pathways. Using BeDA—a multimodal large-language-model auditing tool applied to 2,246 firms over two decades—this study finds that only about one in five built-environment firm reports discloses the required metric. European real-estate firms comply at roughly twice the rate of their US counterparts. Among firms where intensity can be constructed, 39% already exceed the 1.5°C pathway limit. The finding reframes the obstacle to enforceable stranding regulation: it is not a forecasting problem but a measurable, jurisdiction-specific reporting gap that targeted disclosure mandates—monitored by tools like BeDA—could systematically close.
items.centre_angle: This study deploys a multimodal LLM as a large-scale compliance auditing instrument—evaluating thousands of corporate disclosures against a regulatory standard rather than relying on human reviewers. From CAMO's perspective on algorithmic decision support, the work illustrates both the promise and the limits of AI-assisted measurement: BeDA achieves high inter-extractor agreement and convergent validity, but it surfaces a data-quality crisis that no algorithm can resolve on its own. The deeper implication is that AI tools for regulatory compliance are only as useful as the disclosure regimes that feed them—making the design of reporting mandates an organisational and governance question, not just a technical one.

matched_camo.title: Seesaw Experimentation: A/B Tests with Spillovers
matched_camo.reason: Both papers grapple with measurement gaps that distort decisions—BeDA shows that unmeasured or non-standardised disclosure prevents accurate stranding assessment, paralleling how seesaw experimentation shows that optimising a measured primary metric while ignoring unmeasured secondary dimensions leads firms astray.

items.key_takeaway: AI can audit corporate climate disclosures at scale, but four out of five building-sector reports still lack the basic metric—carbon intensity per square metre—that stranding regulation requires, making the reporting gap itself the primary policy problem.
items.visual_concept: A single glass-and-concrete office tower occupies the left third of the frame, shot from street level looking up at a slight angle so the building's vertical lines converge toward a vanishing point high in the upper-right corner, drawing the eye upward. The tower is centred against a pale grey overcast sky kept deliberately empty to avoid competition. Roughly two-thirds of the tower's facade is rendered in sharp, clean white—representing compliant disclosure—while the bottom third fades into a muted, slightly hazy charcoal, suggesting opacity or missing information. The lighting is flat and cool, diffuse northern daylight with no harsh shadows, giving the image a clinical, audit-report quality. The overall palette is restrained: off-white, slate grey, and a single thin red line—a horizontal datum mark drawn across the facade at the compliance threshold—providing the only accent colour.
red_flags: Preprint only—arXiv submission, not yet peer-reviewed; findings should be treated as preliminary.
Audit reliability is demonstrated through inter-extractor agreement and convergent validity but has not been independently replicated by third parties.

The 21.5% compliance figure is based on a region-stratified sample of 200 firm-reports; the broader panel estimate rests on automated extraction whose errors the authors acknowledge but cannot fully quantify at scale.
The paper is primarily a measurement and policy tool contribution; its relevance to AI management and organisational behaviour is indirect, which limits fit with CAMO's core audience.

items.title: Rewired takes: How AI is unlocking creativity and heralding the rise of the agent manager
items.summary: Companies are reassessing how they work, their team structures, and what it means to be a manager in this bracing new era.
items.claude_summary: As AI agents become capable of handling complex, multi-step workflows, companies are rethinking what managers actually do. The McKinsey piece argues that the managerial role is shifting from directing human teams toward orchestrating networks of AI agents — a role it terms the 'agent manager.' Alongside this, AI is portrayed as an enabler of human creativity by absorbing routine cognitive work. The article is based on an RSS excerpt and editorial commentary rather than original research, so specific empirical claims cannot be verified. The core argument is that organizational structures, team compositions, and definitions of managerial accountability are all under active reassessment as agent-based AI moves from pilot to operational deployment.
items.centre_angle: This McKinsey piece argues that AI agents are reshaping the manager's role from supervising people to orchestrating automated systems — a structural shift with real implications for how authority, accountability, and span of control are distributed inside firms. From CAMO's perspective on AI Adoption, the empirical question is whether this reallocation of managerial attention genuinely improves organizational performance or simply displaces accountability without resolving it. CAMO's nano-case on KFC China offers a concrete counterpart: AI-assisted scheduling and demand forecasting freed store managers to oversee larger clusters of stores, but that outcome required deliberate redesign of the managerial role, not just technology deployment.

matched_camo.title: Scaling Managers with AI at KFC China
matched_camo.reason: The KFC China case directly illustrates the 'agent manager' dynamic: AI absorbed routine data-heavy tasks, expanding each manager's effective span of control — providing an empirical reference point for McKinsey's broader claim.

items.authors:

Sam Ransbotham is a professor in the information systems department at the Carroll School of Management at Boston College, as well as guest editor for MIT Sloan Management Review’s Artificial Intelligence and Business Strategy Big Ideas initiative.
items.summary: Erik Brynjolfsson has a challenge for anyone worried about artificial intelligence: Stop asking what AI will do to us, and start asking what we will do with AI. In this episode of Me, Myself, and AI, the Stanford University economist explains why technology isn’t the biggest barrier to progress — people, organizations, and institutions are. […]
items.claude_summary: Economist Erik Brynjolfsson argues that the central barrier to AI-driven prosperity is not the technology itself but the people, organizations, and institutions that shape how it is deployed. Speaking on MIT Sloan's Me, Myself, and AI podcast, he reframes the standard anxiety about AI — what it will do to us — into a design challenge: what choices will we make about how AI is used? The implication is that productivity and distributional outcomes depend heavily on organizational and institutional decisions, not on the capabilities of the models themselves. The excerpt is thin (podcast summary only), so specific empirical claims cannot be verified, but the argument aligns with a well-established strand of labor economics research on technology and complementarity.
items.centre_angle: Brynjolfsson's argument — that organizational and institutional choices, not technical capability, determine AI's economic impact — sits directly alongside CAMO's empirical work on adoption barriers. The Deloitte-HKU AI Adoption Index 2026 found that the dominant barriers among C-suite executives in China and Hong Kong are organisational and executional: siloed departments, cultural resistance, and poor change management, not model performance. The policy implication CAMO would draw is pointed: if shared prosperity is the goal, the design of incentive structures and job architectures around AI matters as much as the AI itself — a point elaborated in CAMO's work on how AI reshapes job quality and agency costs.

items.title: AI in the Australian for-purpose sector: Laying a strong foundation
items.summary: AI adoption in Australian for-purpose organisations is growing, but without a considered approach, AI can add pressure and prioritise output over outcomes. How can leaders prepare their teams for more effective AI journeys?
items.claude_summary: Australian for-purpose organisations—charities, NGOs, and social enterprises—are adopting AI at a growing rate, but the article warns that without deliberate planning, AI risks amplifying operational pressure and optimising for measurable outputs rather than genuine social outcomes. Leaders in this sector face a distinctive challenge: their mission is harder to quantify than profit, making it easy for AI-driven efficiency gains to crowd out the relational, judgment-intensive work that defines their impact. The piece calls on leaders to build considered AI foundations—covering governance, staff readiness, and mission alignment—before scaling deployment. The excerpt is brief and the full argument sits behind McKinsey's site, so specific evidence or data points cannot be confirmed.
items.centre_angle: This article raises a concern that applies well beyond the for-purpose sector: AI adoption guided primarily by efficiency metrics can quietly degrade the quality of work that matters most but is hardest to measure. CAMO's research on seesaw experimentation (Seesaw Experimentation, 2024) formalises exactly this dynamic—innovations that improve a primary measurable dimension can impose unmeasured costs that outweigh the gains. For mission-driven organisations, where outcomes are often relational and long-term, the risk of optimising the measurable at the expense of the meaningful is especially acute, and governance frameworks need to account for it explicitly.

matched_camo.reason: The article's core warning—that AI can improve measured outputs while degrading unmeasured outcomes—maps directly to the seesaw experimentation phenomenon, where optimising a primary metric creates negative spillovers in secondary, harder-to-track dimensions.
